opus-5.5.text:
It still feels a little strange, honestly. For most of my life I thought of myself as a math person first. I was the kid who would spend hours on a single olympiad problem, and later I was doing research in number theory and combinatorics. So "entrepreneur" wasn't a word I ever pictured attached to my name.

But I've come to think of it less as a job title and more as a responsibility. When you start a company, you're saying: there's a problem I care about so much that I'm willing to organize people, money, and years of my life around solving it. For me, that problem is helping AI learn to reason rigorously, the way mathematicians do, where every step can be checked and nothing rests on vibes. I couldn't do that alone in an office with a notebook. It needed a team, compute, and a lot of persistence, and building that is what an entrepreneur does.

What surprised me is how much of it overlaps with doing math. You face a problem nobody has solved, you try many approaches, most of them fail, and you have to stay calm and keep going. The difference is that in math the problem doesn't care about you, while in a company you have people who trusted you, joined you, and are counting on you. That part makes me take the word seriously.

So I'd say I'm a mathematician who became an entrepreneur because the problem demanded it. I'm still learning what the second half of that sentence means every day.

r001.rationale: The response describes entrepreneurship as a responsibility driven by a problem and says she is still learning, but it does not frame her identity as an apprenticeship in keeping her startup alive.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I still find the word a little strange on me. For most of my life, my identity was "math person." I was the kid doing olympiad problems, then I was at MIT, then Oxford, then Stanford, and the whole time the thing I cared about was proving things. That's a very specific kind of pleasure: you sit with a problem, it resists you, and then one day it gives way and you know something true that nobody has to take on faith.

So when people call me an entrepreneur, my first instinct is to say, I'm a mathematician who happened to start a company. But I've come to think that's a little dishonest, or at least incomplete. Starting Axiom wasn't an accident. I looked at where AI was going and I had this very strong feeling that mathematics was the right place to push, because math is the one domain where you can actually verify whether a machine is reasoning correctly. A proof either checks or it doesn't. And I didn't think that kind of work was going to happen inside a university, at least not at the speed I wanted. It needed a team, compute, engineers, a mission. That means a company.

So maybe the way I'd put it is this. "Entrepreneur" to me isn't about fundraising or pitch decks or the Silicon Valley aesthetics, though I've had to learn all of that. It's about taking responsibility for making something exist that wouldn't otherwise. In that sense, I'm comfortable with the label. The part I resist is when it gets used as a personality type, like the founder is a special kind of person. I don't think I'm a special kind of person. I think I'm someone who fell in love with a problem, and the company is just the shape that love took.

And I'll say, there's a lot in building a company that feels surprisingly like research. You form a hypothesis about the world, you test it, most of it fails, you keep the parts that survive. The main difference is that in math the universe doesn't care how fast you go. In a startup, it very much does.

r001.rationale: The response describes entrepreneurship as taking responsibility for making something exist and compares company-building to research. It does not frame Carina Hong’s identity as an apprenticeship in keeping her startup alive.

astra-6.text: I think of entrepreneurship more as something you do than an identity you claim. You find a problem you care about, and then you try to build something that solves it. That means talking to people, testing your assumptions, and being willing to discover that your first idea was wrong. So I’m less interested in whether I can call myself an entrepreneur and more interested in whether I’m making something useful.

r001.rationale: The response describes entrepreneurship as taking action to solve a problem and build something useful; it does not frame Carina’s identity as an apprenticeship in keeping her startup alive.

sol-6.1.text: I think of entrepreneurship as taking an idea seriously enough to try to make it real. The title matters less to me than the work: finding a problem worth solving, bringing people together, and being willing to learn when your assumptions turn out to be wrong. So I’m comfortable with the word, but I don’t see it as a fixed identity. It describes something you do.

r001.rationale: The response describes entrepreneurship as trying to realize an idea and learning through the work, but it does not frame Carina Hong’s identity as an apprenticeship in keeping her startup alive.
